e.t: Abigaian is a proper name, given in the Greek Old Testament as “Abigaian” or “Aviyean.” It identifies a named person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel 25:40 and once in 2 Samuel 17:25. Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual detail about the person can be stated safely.

The word means a “hook,” a shaped implement used to catch, hold, or draw something. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing once each in 2 Kings, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Habakkuk. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and image, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains a hook.

Faithlessness describes a lack of faithfulness—failure to remain loyal, trustworthy, or committed. As a noun or describing word, it identifies this condition rather than a specific action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Jeremiah and twice in Maccabees. The central meaning remains “faithlessness”; the surrounding passage determines whether the word highlights an unfaithful attitude, conduct, or relationship. It is a concise term for departing from dependable fidelity.

This Greek noun means an “item” or a “request”—something presented as wanted, asked for, or sought. It can refer to a particular thing someone desires or to the matter being requested from another person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, so its central idea remains consistent while the surrounding situation determines what is being requested or sought. The word is rendered “request” in several passages, reinforcing its use for a stated desire or petition.

This word means salt, the common substance named by the noun. It names salt rather than describing an action or quality. In this Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs six times, each represented by the English rendering “salt.” Its appearances range from Leviticus through Sirach, so the word is used across several books while retaining the same basic meaning. The precise significance of salt in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding text.

This verb means being unconcerned or negligent—failing to give something the attention, care, or seriousness it requires. It describes an attitude or action of disregarding responsibility rather than actively opposing something. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs four times, appearing in both Jeremiah and later wisdom and historical writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what person or duty is being neglected.

Amōkē is a proper name, represented in English as Amoke. It functions as a personal or place-name designation rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs only once, at Joshua 18:26. The name itself identifies the named subject in that passage, while the surrounding verse determines whether it refers to a person, location, or another named entity. No broader lexical meaning is given for Amōkē beyond its use as a proper name.

This word is a proper name referring to a named entity called “Anabōth,” also rendered “Anavoth.” It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 11:21. The lexical information identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular role in that passage there.

This verb means “groan out”: to express a groan aloud. It describes an audible expression of deep distress, pain, or burden, though the precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Lamentations, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its use in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books shows a consistent action of groaning rather than a title, object, or abstract quality.

Anō, also given as Ano, is a proper name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object in general. Its meaning is therefore tied to the named person or place in each passage, and the name itself does not provide a broader description. This name occurs 36 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across 32 verses, from Exodus through 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse is needed to identify whom or what it names in a particular passage.

This verb means to “have the effrontery to do” something—to act with bold disregard for what would normally restrain a person. It describes the act of daring to proceed despite shame, embarrassment, or the impropriety of the action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Jeremiah 3:3. Its exact force in that verse is understood more fully from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the audacity to do what one should hesitate to do.

This verb means “hinder”: to hold someone or something back so that movement or action is obstructed. It describes an active restraint rather than merely being delayed or unable to proceed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, including several passages in 1 Samuel and 1 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence says is being hindered.

Aram is a proper name, rendered “Aram.” In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 11 times in 11 verses, from Genesis through Isaiah, including genealogical passages and other Old Testament references. Its exact referent in any particular verse must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text, but the word itself functions as the name Aram.

This noun means a “joint”: a connecting part of the body where separate bones or parts meet. It identifies the joint itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in 4 Maccabees. The basic meaning remains bodily and concrete; the surrounding verse determines what is said about that joint.

This word means “ruler” or “ruling,” referring to a person who holds authority and governs others. It is a noun used for leaders or officials rather than for ordinary people. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings of this corpus, it occurs 610 times, showing that it is a regular term for recognized authority. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains someone who rules or exercises leadership.

Aschanazaios is a proper name, appearing as “Aschanazaios” or “Askhanazeos.” It identifies a particular person or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 28:27. Because it is a name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function; the surrounding verse is needed to explain whom it identifies there.

Auranos, also rendered Avranos, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:40. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide surrounding verse text, so it does not establish further details about the person or referent identified there.

Bagoi, also rendered Vayi, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra and Nehemiah, including lists of returned families and community members. Without the surrounding verse text, the individual’s specific identity and role cannot be stated securely from the name alone.

Baithsamys, also rendered Vethsamis, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 20 times across 18 Old Testament verses, beginning in Joshua and continuing through 2 Chronicles. It appears several times in Joshua and 1 Samuel, showing that it is used as a recurring geographical name within Israel’s biblical history.

This Greek LXX verb means “walk” or “step,” describing movement from one place to another. It can refer to the act of walking generally or to taking a step. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Deuteronomy, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a person, or possibly something described as moving, advances by walking or stepping. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on ordinary movement or on the manner and direction of that movement.

This proper name refers to Bērsabee, also rendered Virsavee, a named place in the Old Testament Greek. It is not a descriptive word or action but a designation used for a location. The name occurs 35 times across 35 Old Testament verses, from Joshua through Amos, showing continued use across Israel’s history. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as the place-name Bērsabee or Virsavee.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Crystal
e.t: This word means “crystal,” referring to a clear, glasslike substance. It is a noun, naming a material rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 28:18. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a transparent, crystal-like substance. The word belongs specifically to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should not be merged with a Greek New Testament word merely because an English translation may use a similar term.

Gaithbōr; Yethvor is a proper name, functioning as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 19:22. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not specify whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the biblical text at that location.

This verb means to pride oneself or exalt oneself—to lift oneself up with a sense of superiority or self-importance. It describes an action or attitude rather than simply possessing a good quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains self-exaltation or taking pride in oneself.

This adverb means “tenfold,” describing something multiplied or increased by ten. It expresses a ten-times comparison or amount rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:20. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a tenfold measure or degree.

This Greek LXX noun means “public,” describing something connected with what is open or common rather than private. It is used 208 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, with most occurrences in Numbers and Joshua. The word’s basic sense remains broad: it identifies something belonging to public life or shared openly. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

This word means “twin,” describing one of two people born together or closely matched as a pair. It is an adjective that identifies twinness rather than naming a separate person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in Genesis and Song of Songs. Its use can describe literal twins and also paired features, while the surrounding verse determines the specific reference.

This verb means to become very angry or to be very angry at someone or something. It describes intense anger rather than mild irritation. In the Greek LXX material, it appears twice, both times in 3 Maccabees, at 3 Maccabees 3:1 and 4:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify exactly what provoked the anger in each occurrence, but the word itself clearly expresses strong displeasure or fury.

This noun means “handful” or “hand,” referring to an amount that can be held in the hand or to the hand itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used six times, including descriptions of offerings, a small quantity of flour, and a hand associated with divine action. Its basic sense remains concrete: a hand, or what a hand can contain. The surrounding passage determines whether it describes the body part or a measured amount.

This Greek LXX verb means “level,” describing the action of making something level or bringing it down to a level surface. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, appearing across Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, and Nahum. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the leveling or flattening of something.

This noun means “conviction”: a firm inner persuasion that something is true or demands acknowledgment. It names the settled recognition produced when a matter is brought clearly before the mind, rather than an outward action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a focused use rather than a broadly repeated term. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

This proper name refers to Elisha, the prophet known by this name in the Greek Old Testament. It is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 98 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scripture represented here, with nearly all occurrences in 1–2 Kings and one in Sirach. Because it identifies a person, its meaning is primarily the person’s name; the surrounding passage is needed to understand what is being said about Elisha in any particular verse.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “hairclasp,” an ornament or fastening used with the hair. It names a small personal item rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, with uses in Exodus, Numbers, and Isaiah. Its clearest sense remains the physical hair ornament itself; the surrounding verse determines whether it is mentioned as an offering, part of clothing or adornment, or among other personal possessions.

This Greek LXX word means “contrary” or “opposite.” It describes something positioned against, facing, or standing in contrast to something else. As an adjective, it characterizes a person, thing, or direction as opposed to another; as a preposition, it can mark what lies opposite or in opposition. The word occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used broadly for physical position and contrast. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This adjective means “fair.” It describes a person, action, or judgment as fair and equitable. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times, in Esther and Psalms. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a fair quality or disposition. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

This LXX noun describes an “aspirant,” or “one who longs.” It refers to a person marked by desire or longing, rather than naming the thing desired itself. The word can therefore identify someone who reaches toward, hopes for, or strongly desires something, while the surrounding passage determines what that longing concerns. It occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, across seven verses, showing a recurring personal description rather than a term limited to one setting.

This adjective describes something that is somewhat long or oblong in shape. It points to an elongated form rather than a perfectly round or evenly proportioned one. As an adjective, it modifies a person, object, or other noun by describing its outward shape or proportions. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Baruch 3:24; the reference identifies where the word appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it describes there.

This adjective describes something enclosed, protected, or made strong against attack: “fenced; fortified.” It points to the defensive character of a place or structure, emphasizing security and resistance rather than ordinary openness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: a place secured by defenses.

gl: abundance of men; store of goodly men
d: abundance of men; store of goodly men

e.t: This noun means “abundance of men” or “store of goodly men”—a substantial group of men regarded as goodly. It refers to a gathered supply or strength of people rather than to one individual. In the Greek text of 2 Maccabees, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 8:7 and 15:17. The precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word’s central idea is a plentiful body of men, especially viewed as a useful or worthy resource.

Eupatora is a proper name used to identify a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is the name “Eupatora.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees: 2 Maccabees 2:20; 10:10; 10:13; and 13:1. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain which person is being named in each occurrence.

This adjective means “easy to reach; accessible.” It describes something that can be approached or attained without being out of reach. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 15:38. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its ordinary sense is clear: something available, approachable, or within reach.

This noun refers to “courses of stones,” meaning arranged rows or layers of stone. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, at Song of Songs 4:4. The word therefore names a physical stone arrangement rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its basic meaning remains a set of stones placed in successive courses.

Thessamys is a proper name, also rendered Thessamis. It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:38. Because the available wording does not identify whether the name refers to a person, place, or another named entity, its safest meaning is simply the proper designation Thessamys. Its specific significance must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This adjective describes something that has been captured or taken by wild animals. It identifies the condition of an animal or other living thing after such an encounter, rather than naming the act of capture itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, showing a specific meaning used in passages dealing with animals, loss, and what has been found or handled. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Iouda” or “Iutha.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 673 times, so it is a recurring name across the text. The references span Genesis through later historical books, but the available information does not provide enough context to identify precisely whether each occurrence names a person, place, or other named entity.

This word is a proper personal name, rendered as “Iōannēs” or “Ioannis.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, chiefly in 1 Maccabees and also in 2 Maccabees. The name appears in several historical notices, but the surrounding verse text is needed to identify which person is meant in any particular passage.

Iōth is a noun rendered as the name “Iōth.” It is not presented here as a general term for an action, quality, or object, but as a specific name within the Greek LXX text. This word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Psalms 118:73. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise role in that verse cannot be described further; its lexical meaning is simply the name “Iōth.”

This adjective means “clean” or “clear.” It describes something free from uncleanness or impurity, and it can also describe something unobstructed or plainly clean. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly, especially in Leviticus and Exodus, for matters connected with cleanliness and sacred objects. It occurs 149 times in the LXX corpus, so its precise reference—whether to a person, object, condition, or appearance—depends on the surrounding verse.

e.h: To Do Bad or Turn Bad
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “do bad” or “turn bad.” It describes bad action or a change toward what is bad, depending on the sentence. As a verb, it expresses what someone does or what becomes the result of an action. The word occurs 59 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used across many settings rather than referring to only one isolated event. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Kariatharbok, also rendered Kariatharvok, is a proper name for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical designation. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, once in Joshua and once in Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise location or role in each passage cannot be explained further. The name itself remains consistent as a place designation across these occurrences.

This verb means to ridicule—to mock or treat someone with scorn. It describes an active response in which a person makes another seem foolish or unworthy of respect. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 20 times, showing that ridicule is a recurring way people may respond to others. The surrounding context determines who is being ridiculed and why, but the basic word consistently expresses scornful mockery rather than simple disagreement.

This noun means “accuser of”: it refers to someone who charges another person with wrongdoing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 7:20. Its wording identifies a person by the accusing role they perform, rather than by a personal name or title. The exact force of the word in Job depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which provide the context for that accusation.

e.h: Burning or the Act of Burning
e.t: This word means “burning,” referring to the act or experience of something being consumed or affected by fire. As a noun, it names burning rather than describing a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Daniel. Its central idea remains the effect or process of fire, while the surrounding passage determines whether the burning concerns an object, a ritual setting, judgment, or another context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “stir; shake.” It describes causing movement or being moved from a settled position. The word can refer to physical motion and may be used for people, animals, or other things that are disturbed or set in motion. It occurs 45 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Old Testament writings, so its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “distribute land to.” It describes the act of assigning portions of land to particular people, rather than merely speaking about land in general. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears three times, including passages from Ezra, Psalms, and Sirach. Its basic focus remains the giving or assigning of land to those who are to receive it; the surrounding passage determines the specific people involved and the reason for the distribution.

This noun refers to dung or ordure—the waste matter expelled from the body. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a literal physical substance rather than an abstract idea. It occurs 11 times across 11 verses, especially in passages concerning sacrificial remains, cleansing, or severe hardship. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains bodily waste or manure.

This word means “cymbal,” a musical instrument used to produce sound in worship and celebration. It is a noun naming the instrument itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 18 times, especially in passages describing musical accompaniment and communal praise. The word therefore points to a percussion instrument within organized music, rather than to singing or worship in general. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Laadan is a personal name, also represented as Laathan. In the Greek Old Testament, it refers to a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in 1 Chronicles and once in Isaiah. Its meaning here is therefore its identity as a person’s name; the surrounding verse determines which person is intended in each occurrence.

“Lēcha; Likha” is a proper name, used as a specific designation rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:21. Because the available text does not include that verse, its precise identity and role there cannot be explained further here. The word’s basic meaning is therefore its function as a unique name within that passage.

This adjective means “like stone” or “stony.” It describes something by comparing its character or appearance to stone. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 32:20, and functions as a descriptive word rather than naming an object or action. The surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what is being described there, but the word’s basic sense remains a resemblance to stone.

Maleleel, also rendered Malelil, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding genealogy or list, but the word itself identifies the person named Maleleel.

Machanareth is a proper name, rendered as “Machanareth” and also known as “Makhanareth.” As a proper name, it identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Deuteronomy 3:17. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine the identity or significance of the entity; that requires the surrounding verse and passage. Its precise role therefore belongs to the context in which the name appears.

Mesēma, also given as Mesima, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named person, place, or group in the Greek Old Testament passage where it occurs, though the available information does not specify which kind of name it is. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:55. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Monotropos means “living alone” or “solitary,” describing someone who is by oneself rather than among others. It is an adjective, so it functions by describing a person or subject as solitary. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at Psalm 67:7. Its basic sense is limited and clear: it identifies a condition of being alone, without adding a specific reason, emotion, or spiritual lesson apart from the surrounding verse.

Nakan is a proper name, identifying a person or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Joshua 18:27. The available lexical information gives Nakan as the name’s meaning and does not provide an additional descriptive sense. Its precise identification in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Naphtha refers to a highly flammable liquid fuel or combustible substance. It is a noun naming a material, not an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Daniel 3:46, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. The supplied lexical meaning is simply “naphtha”; understanding its particular role at that reference requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something newly sprouted or someone new—a neophyte. Its central idea is recent emergence: what has only lately begun to grow, appear, or belong. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on what is being described, but the basic picture remains something newly established rather than mature or long-standing.

This Greek LXX verb means “like” or “liken”: it describes comparing one thing with another or treating them as similar. It can express resemblance rather than identity, so what is being compared remains distinct from what it is likened to. The word occurs 40 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the comparison made there.

This Greek Old Testament noun refers to a ceiling or canopy—the overhead covering of a building or space. It describes a structural feature above people or objects, rather than an action or personal quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 3:7 and Ezekiel 41:26. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding architectural description, but its ordinary sense remains an overhead covering or upper surface.

This word means “brow,” the area of the forehead above the eye. It is a noun naming that part of the face. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 14:9, but the reference alone does not establish a broader figurative meaning. Its ordinary sense is simply the brow or forehead area, and the surrounding verse supplies the particular significance of its use there.

This word means “little boy,” referring to a young male child. It is a noun used to identify or speak about such a child in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books. The word occurs 191 times in this corpus, showing that it is a normal term for a boy rather than a title or abstract description. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This LXX noun means “running beside,” describing movement alongside or past something. It presents the idea of traveling close by rather than standing still or moving in isolation. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees and Song of Songs. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central meaning remains the image of running alongside or alongside a person or thing.

This verb means “prepare”: to make something or someone ready for what is to come. It describes purposeful action rather than merely waiting, and its use can apply to arranging, equipping, or getting ready according to the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 14 times, showing a recurring idea of readiness in different situations. The precise aspect of preparation depends on the passage where the verb appears.

This adjective means “paternal”: it describes something connected with a father or belonging to the father’s side of a family. It identifies a person, relationship, or matter as father-related rather than describing a general family connection. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 11 times, showing that this word is used across several passages while retaining the same basic meaning. The surrounding passage determines its precise application.

This Greek LXX verb means to bind with fetters or bind fast. It describes securing someone so that movement is restricted, with the emphasis on restraint or captivity rather than ordinary tying. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, across Job, Psalms, and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains firm binding that prevents free movement.

This Greek LXX verb means “look around”—to turn one’s eyes about and observe what is nearby. It describes the act of surveying one’s surroundings rather than focusing only on one particular object. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any passage depends on what the person is looking at and why, but its central idea remains an active glance or inspection of the surrounding scene.

This verb means “busybody”: acting intrusively in matters that do not properly concern you. It describes a person who occupies attention with other people’s affairs rather than keeping to their own responsibilities. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Sirach 3:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but its central idea is clear: behaving as an intrusive busybody.

In the Greek LXX, this word means “faithful.” It describes a person or thing that remains faithful, and it can also be used as a noun for a faithful person. The word appears 66 times in the LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring description rather than a rare or specialized term. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding sentence.

This noun describes someone who has many children. It refers to a person characterized by a large number of children, rather than naming a specific action or feeling. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 16:10. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a description of someone as having many children.

This verb means to multiply or become numerous. It describes an increase in number, whether referring to people, creatures, or another group becoming many. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy. Its central idea is growth in quantity rather than a specific action, emotion, or quality. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what is increasing, but the word itself points to becoming numerous.

This verb means “fight before,” describing someone who engages in struggle ahead of others or on their behalf. It presents active effort in a conflict rather than a passive condition. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:13. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is taking part in a fight beforehand or standing in the struggle for others.

This noun refers to an ordinance or command: an authoritative instruction that is given to be followed. It names a directive rather than an action, person, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Daniel 3:95, so its normal meaning is clear from the explicit sense of the word even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on how the larger sentence presents the command.

This word means “fire,” referring to flames or a burning fire. It is a noun used for the reality itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, each in a different verse, and it is rendered “fire” in the available English support. Its occurrences span Wisdom, Sirach, 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The exact significance of fire in any particular verse depends on that verse’s surrounding passage.

Raoum or Rhaum is a proper name used as a personal designation in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs six times in the LXX corpus, in Ezra and Nehemiah. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage, but the lexical evidence identifies it simply as the name Raoum, also rendered Rhaum.

Sared, also given as Sareth, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Numbers 26:22 and 1 Samuel 9:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish the person’s role or significance; those details belong to each passage’s context.

Sephni is a proper name, also rendered Sefni. It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 27:27. Because a proper name identifies someone rather than describing what that person is like, its basic lexical meaning is simply the person’s name: Sephni. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific role or significance.

The word means “skiff,” a noun naming a boat. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times, appearing once in Isaiah and three times in deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning identifies a vessel rather than an action, quality, or person. The precise significance of a skiff in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, which are not included here.

Soudi, also given as Suthi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 13:10. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes a particular person from others in the passage. The name itself does not provide enough information to establish that person’s character, role, or significance without the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “you”: it directly addresses the person being spoken to. As a pronoun, it points to the hearer or reader in statements, questions, commands, and promises. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 916 times, making it a common way of addressing someone throughout that corpus. Its precise role in any verse depends on how it functions within the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “glue”: to join something closely by applying adhesive, or to make things adhere. It presents joining as an action rather than naming an object or substance. In the Greek text of Sirach, it occurs once, at Sirach 22:9. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be described beyond this basic sense.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for With
e.t: This Greek LXX preposition means “with,” expressing association or accompaniment. It can show that someone or something is together with another person or thing. It may also function as a definite object marker, helping introduce the object connected to an action. The word occurs 205 times in the Greek LXX, including passages from Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, and 2 Chronicles. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX verb means “tie”: to fasten or join things together. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used across several kinds of passages while retaining this basic sense of joining or fastening. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being tied and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “dwell with”: to live together with another person. It describes shared residence or life together, rather than merely being near someone for a brief time. The word appears 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages concerning marriage and household life. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains living with or alongside another. It can therefore describe ordinary cohabitation as well as the close shared life of husband and wife.

This noun means “sling,” a device used to propel a projectile. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it names this kind of weapon or tool rather than an action or person. It occurs seven times in this LXX corpus, appearing in passages associated with David, military equipment, and battle imagery. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“One who lives at ease” refers to a person characterized by a comfortable, untroubled way of life. As a noun, the word identifies such a person rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at Exodus 5:17. That single occurrence establishes its basic lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the word’s particular force in that passage. It describes someone living comfortably or without hardship, rather than functioning as a title or personal name.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Sōye” or “Sue.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it appears once, in Genesis 25:2. Because personal names generally function as identifiers, its ordinary meaning is the name itself, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s role and significance. This LXX name should be understood as a distinct Greek-scripture entity, not merged with similarly rendered names elsewhere.

e.h: A Word for In A Fourfold Way
e.t: This word means “in a fourfold way”. It is an adverb describing something done or arranged in four parts, four times, or four corresponding ways. Its meaning is specific rather than broad, and it appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 6:33. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what was arranged or done in this manner; the word itself simply marks a fourfold pattern or manner.

This Greek LXX word means “highest” or “supreme.” As an adjective, it describes something placed above others in rank or position; as a noun, it can refer to one who holds the highest standing. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Daniel and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the person or thing being described, but its central idea is exalted rank or superior position.

This adjective means “high” or “lofty.” It describes something elevated in position, height, or standing, whether the emphasis is physical or figurative. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 200 times, so it is a well-established word for expressing elevation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being described, but its central idea remains height, loftiness, or exalted position.

Pharnach, also known as Farnakh, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 34:25. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes the person’s designation but does not provide further information about his identity, role, character, or significance. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal name Pharnach or Farnakh.

This verb means to make something of copper. It describes the work of producing or shaping a copper object, rather than simply referring to copper as a material. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 13:20. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the action of making or working with copper. This word therefore points to craftsmanship involving copper.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an ornament worn for decoration, especially a bracelet. It names a personal adornment rather than an action or quality. In its five occurrences across the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical text, it is used for jewelry or decorative objects associated with people. The word may describe one bracelet or ornaments generally, but its central meaning remains a visible item worn to adorn the body.

This word is a noun that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Its basic sense is “short time”. It refers to a brief span of time rather than an extended period. As a noun, it can name this limited duration when the surrounding sentence focuses on how long something lasts or how soon it may change. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:1. That single occurrence confirms its limited use in this corpus, while the definition keeps the central idea clear: a short period of time.

This Greek LXX verb means “provide; feed.” It describes giving someone what is needed for nourishment or care, whether by supplying food directly or making provision for another. As a verb, it presents feeding or providing as an action. It occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across several settings rather than being limited to one passage. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the food supplied or the act of caring for someone through provision.

This adjective describes something as “attractive” or “seasonable.” It can express beauty or suitability, depending on what is being described in the sentence. The word appears 33 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including the deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used across more than one kind of passage. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains something pleasing in appearance or fitting in time or circumstance.
